newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek Premier gambles all on early election.
newsitem.headline: Greek Premier gambles all on early election.

text.p: Greece's socialist Prime Minister Costas Simitis will cement his grip on power in early elections next Sunday or see his sudden political rise come to an equally abrupt end.
Simitis, 60, took the reins of his Panhellenic Socialist Movement (PASOK) in January while its founder and long-time leader Andreas Papandreou lay mortally ill.

He called the vote confident of an easy win over the divided opposition conservatives, but widespread voter apathy and a strong showing by smaller leftist parties have pushed him into a neck-and-neck race.

Polls show both Simitis and conservative New Democracy party leader Miltiades Evert hovering around 31 percent, reflecting a sharp fall in the popularity of the parties which have dominated politics for 20 years.
Simitis, a deadpan academic who abhors Greece's penchant for demagogues, started the race a strong favourite but his distant bearing and dry style compared to Papandreou have left many voters cold.

"He's a goal-oriented methodical administrator, who believes a firm, quiet, organised approach is the way forward. He doesn't like campaigning and, unfortunately, that's clear to us all," a socialist party official said.
Simitis was elected party leader on demands for reform after years of autocratic Papandreou rule.

But he has done little to fire socialist passions and has confused leftists with his neo-conservative approach to the economy, determination to meet stringent EU targets and his clear message the days of free-spending socialism were over.
That has fueled the fortunes of smaller left-wing parties, which are bleeding off Simitis's votes and raising hopes among Evert's conservatives that a major upset could be in the offing.

"The wild cards are the smaller leftist parties -- whether they draw off crucial votes from Simitis or their support dries up and voters go home to PASOK next Sunday," said one European Union diplomat who has been tracking the race.
Opinion polls show a race too close to call but they also show a heavy majority of those questioned believing Simitis, whose personal popularity has always towered above Evert, will triumph.
Indeed, it is difficult to find a polling expert, diplomat, stock market analyst or banker who is not predicting a Simitis win by two percentage points or more.
That is largely because Evert, too, appears to have failed to inspire the sea of unhappy voters with his podium-thumping style and string of campaign pledges.
Evert, 57, made his name as mayor of Athens in the 1980's, who broke the state monopoly of television and radio and was dubbed "the Bulldozer" for getting the job done.

He is handicapped by having only the shrinking nationalist Political Spring party to woo voters from. To that end he has attacked Simitis for retreating in a row with with Turkey in January over disputed Aegean islands.
His angry denunciations of Simitis's handling of the crisis, which saw the Greek flag removed from an uninhabited island, are aimed clearly at courting Political Spring voters.
